title: Valid Anagram
pattern: Count letters with a hash map
statement: Given two strings `s` and `t`, return `True` if `t` is an **anagram** of `s` — it uses exactly the same letters the same number of times, just in a different order.

example.why: Both words contain a×1, p×2, l×1, e×1.

picture: Picture two bags of letter tiles. Tip out the first bag and count its tiles: two `p`s, one `a`, and so on. Then take the tiles of the second bag one by one and cross off a matching tile from your count. If you ever need a tile that is not left, the two words do not use the same letters.
idea: Two words are anagrams when every letter appears the same number of times in both.
Count the letters of `s` in a hash map: letter → how many.
Then walk through `t` and *use up* one count per letter. If a letter is missing or already used up, it is not an anagram. Equal lengths guarantee nothing is left over at the end.

say.1: LeetCode puts every answer inside a class named `Solution`. It is only a wrapper: the real work happens in the function below it.
say.2: The function we must write. It gets two words, `s` and `t`, and answers `True` or `False`.
say.3: `len` counts the letters of a word. If the two lengths are different (`!=`), the words cannot be made of the same letters.
say.6: Make an empty **dictionary** (a hash map). It will pair each letter with how many times it appears in `s`.
say.9: Go through the first word, one letter at a time.
say.10: Add one to this letter's count. `.get(char, 0)` means: the count so far, or 0 if the letter has not appeared yet.
say.13: Now go through the second word, one letter at a time.
say.14: Is this letter missing from the counts, or are its copies all used up (count 0)?
say.15: Yes: `t` needs a letter that `s` has no copy of to spare, so answer `False`.
say.16: Use up one copy of this letter: its count goes down by one (`-=` means *subtract and keep the result*).
say.18: Every letter of `t` was matched and the lengths are equal, so nothing is left over: answer `True`.

complexity.timeWhy: One pass over `s` to count and one pass over `t` to match.
complexity.spaceWhy: The map holds at most one entry per distinct letter (26 for lowercase English).

steps.text: Our example: **`s = "apple", t = "papel"`**. Each step runs one highlighted line of the code.
Both strings have 5 letters, so they *could* be anagrams. (Different lengths would mean **False** immediately.)
Create a map that will count how many times each letter appears in `s`.
Count `a` from `s`: the map now has 1 of it.
Count `p` from `s`: the map now has 1 of it.
Count `p` from `s`: the map now has 2 of it.
Count `l` from `s`: the map now has 1 of it.
Count `e` from `s`: the map now has 1 of it.
The map now describes `s` exactly. Next, walk through `t` and **use up** one count for each letter.
`p` from `t`: the map still has 2 of it, so it can be matched. Use one up → 1 left.
`a` from `t`: the map still has 1 of it, so it can be matched. Use one up → 0 left.
`p` from `t`: the map still has 1 of it, so it can be matched. Use one up → 0 left.
`e` from `t`: the map still has 1 of it, so it can be matched. Use one up → 0 left.
`l` from `t`: the map still has 1 of it, so it can be matched. Use one up → 0 left.
Every letter of `t` found a partner, and the lengths are equal, so nothing is left over. They are anagrams → **True**.
Done — the answer is **`True`**. Both words contain a×1, p×2, l×1, e×1.
